name: Western Durango Nahuatl
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Canger, Una (2001) Mexicanero de la Sierra Madre Occidental. Archivo de Lenguas Indigenas de Mexico 24, El Colegio de Mexico (ALIM online viewer lists the volume but its page scans 404).

new_statements.quote: He encontrado la pérdida total de la duración vocálica contrastiva en un solo dialecto, el de Durango. Diré que en este dialecto la influencia ha avanzado aún más: la sílaba prominente se pronuncia más fuertemente y participa en la morfología de la misma manera que en el español, donde la reconocemos, por ejemplo, en la diferencia entre tomo y tomó. Ejemplos de este fenómeno en el nauatl de Durango serían los siguientes: taxkál (tortilla) vs no-táxkal (mi tortilla), ki-tás (lo tira) vs ki-tasá (lo tiraba). [...] Sabemos que hoy en día los hablantes de todos los dialectos del nauatl pronuncian sus palabras con más fuerza en la penúltima sílaba.
new_statements.translation: I have found the total loss of contrastive vowel length in only one dialect, that of Durango. I would say that in this dialect the influence has advanced even further: the prominent syllable is pronounced more strongly and takes part in the morphology in the same way as in Spanish, where we recognize it, for example, in the difference between tomo and tomó. Examples of this phenomenon in Durango Nahuatl would be the following: taxkál (tortilla) vs no-táxkal (my tortilla), ki-tás (he throws it) vs ki-tasá (he was throwing it). [...] We know that today the speakers of all Nahuatl dialects pronounce their words with more force on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Canger, Una. 2018. ¿Por qué los topónimos México y Chapultepec tienen acento en la primera y en la última sílaba? Estudios de Cultura Náhuatl 56: 87-95. México: UNAM, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable, as in all modern Nahuatl varieties; but in the Durango (San Agustín de Buenaventura) variety, which has lost contrastive vowel length, stress has become mobile and grammatically contrastive: apocopated nouns and certain verb forms (imperfect/preterite, plural-subject -l, plural -m) carry surface final stress (taxkál vs no-táxkal; ki-tás vs ki-tasá; síwat vs siwám), and per Canger 2000 the antepenult is occasionally stressed too. Canger 2000 frames this as either (A) a penultimate default plus morphologically loaded stress rules (adverbs: final if consonant-final, penult if vowel-final; some nouns ad hoc), or (B) a phonological penultimate rule (not counting enclitics) applied before syncope of underlying word-final vowels (taxkál-me, siwá-m). The fixed-penult label is the default rule with substantial morphological exceptions; lexical-unpredictable would overstate it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress on apocopated nouns and on morphologically marked verb forms (imperfect/past, plural subject) and consonant-final adverbs; occasional antepenultimate stress (Canger 2000 snippet); Canger 2000 says the raw example list 'points to no restrictions at all on stress assignment'. Canger attributes the whole pattern to Spanish influence.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (single words and inflected forms, citation and text forms); Canger 2018 speaks of 'el dialecto de Durango' generically, the data being her San Agustín de Buenaventura fieldwork (fn. 13 = Canger 2000). Canger 2000's Description B refers to enclitics not counting for the penult rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Canger's Durango data come from San Agustín de Buenaventura, Mezquital, Durango = Western Durango Nahuatl (west2778, ISO azn), which the ISO 2011-111 split also groups with Santa Cruz/Acaponeta, Nayarit. Canger 2018 says only 'el dialecto de Durango' but its fn. 13 points to Canger 2000, whose fieldwork site is San Buenaventura. The Preuss/Ziehm/Castro Medina/Reyes Taboada literature on San Pedro Jícora (Xícoras) is the sister variety Eastern Durango Nahuatl (east2695, azd), which shares the mobile-stress pattern but differs phonetically and morphologically (Reyes Taboada & Villa Reyes 2023, fn. 3). Canger 2001 (ALIM 24) covers only San Buenaventura.

sources.locator: pp. 93-94 (Durango paragraph p. 93 with fn. 13 = Canger 2000; general penult sentence p. 94)
sources.note: Whole article is on Nahuatl word prosody. p.93: all modern Nahuatl dialects stress the penultimate syllable (Spanish influence), but Durango is the one dialect that has lost contrastive vowel length entirely and there 'la sílaba prominente se pronuncia más fuertemente y participa en la morfología de la misma manera que en el español'; examples taxkál 'tortilla' vs no-táxkal 'my tortilla', ki-tás 'he throws it' vs ki-tasá 'he was throwing it'; fn.13 cites Canger 2000 (= San Agustín de Buenaventura fieldwork, west2778). p.94: 'hoy en día los hablantes de todos los dialectos del nauatl pronuncia…

Gramática section: 'Una de las mayores diferencias es el acento prosódico que en algunos casos participa en el sistema morfológico' [ref: Canger 2001: 29], kitása 'lo avienta' vs kitasá 'lo aventó'; researchers write no accent on paroxytones and mark only oxytones, mostly past-tense verb forms with reduced roots. Tertiary; used only as a page pointer into Canger 2001 (file saved anyway).

sources.citation: Pharao Hansen, Magnus. 2024. Sapir's Law and the role of accent in the reconstruction of Proto-Corachol-Nahuan. International Journal of American Linguistics 90(2), doi:10.1086/728639 (accepted manuscript, OSF doi:10.31219/osf.io/zrh2m)
sources.note: Manuscript p.17 (accent survey section), second-hand with the glottocode named: 'Canger (2000) has also shown that in some Nahuan varieties such as Durango Nahual (mexicanero, ISO:azn; Glottolog:west2778), stress has become mobile following the loss of certain vowels: for example síwat "woman" but siwám "women".' Also: Nahuan varieties today generally have fixed penultimate stress; Canger 2018 argues that is post-colonial.

sources.note: Sister variety San Pedro de Xícoras (east2695, azd), not west2778: pp.120-121 stress not always penult, has grammatical functions (citing Canger 2000, Castro Medina 2000); p.124 accent written on every non-penult form; fn.3 warns Canger 2001 covers only San Buenaventura, which differs phonetically and morphologically. Read for identity control only.

sources.note: Text from Santa Cruz/Saycota, Acaponeta, Nayarit (azn = west2778). p.181, second-hand on Canger's San Agustín Buenaventura work: 'También aborda el tema del acento y su función gramatical (Canger, 2000) que, a diferencia de otras variedades, en el mexicanero no cae en la penúltima sílaba, sino que es parte del sistema morfológico.' No rule of its own.
